meta.title: Who really said "If voting made any difference, they wouldn't let us do it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain. This line appears in none of his works; the Twain tag dates only to 2008. It is an anonymous 1960s–80s activist slogan.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If voting made any difference, they wouldn't let us do it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mark Twain. It's an anonymous 20th-century activist slogan—the Twain misattribution only appears online from 2008.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — a 20th-century activist slogan
answer.authorDates: Origin unknown · in circulation by the 1960s–1980s
answer.sourceLine: This is not Twain. The line is absent from his books, letters, and recorded speeches, and Robert Hirst, curator of the Mark Twain Papers at UC Berkeley, flatly answered “absolutely not” when asked if Twain said it ↗. It reads as an anonymous anarchist/activist slogan from the 1960s onward — variously credited to Berkeley radicals like Travus T. Hipp and Bob Avakian — that was only pinned on Twain in the social-media era ↗.

source.heading: Where the slogan actually comes from

docMeta.dd: A tweet on US Election Day, 2008

source.excerpt: “If voting made any difference, they wouldn’t let us do it.”
trail: The Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗ finds no instance of the line associated with Twain before a 2008 Election-Day tweet, and traces it to 1960s Berkeley radicals.
FactCheck.org ↗ quotes Robert Hirst, curator of the Mark Twain Papers, saying “absolutely not” — and notes Twain actually praised “the ballot box.”
The slogan predates the meme: Ken Livingstone’s 1987 autobiography carried the ironic title If Voting Changed Anything They’d Abolish It ↗.
source.excerptNote: The wording is unstable — it also circulates as “If voting changed anything, they’d make it illegal” and “…it would never be allowed,” a telltale sign of a slogan with no fixed source. British politician Ken Livingstone borrowed the form for his 1987 memoir If Voting Changed Anything, They’d Abolish It.

sourceLink.text: Center for Mark Twain Studies: The Apocryphal Twain

source.rightsNote: No fixed source or single author has ever been documented for this slogan, and its wording varies from citation to citation, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted. It is not a Mark Twain text; the real Twain works are public-domain, but this line is not among them.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: The name the slogan borrows
author.bio: Mark Twain (Samuel Langhorne Clemens) was America’s foremost humorist and the author of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. His mordant wit makes him a magnet for invented political one-liners, but on voting the real Twain was earnest: in a 1905 interview he called the ballot box “the finest asset we’ve got.” He died in 1910 — decades before this slogan surfaced — and it appears nowhere in his vast published and archived output.

misattribution.heading: A slogan in search of an author
misattribution.intro: This aphorism is a fake-quote magnet: it has been hung on several famous names, none of whom can be shown to have said it. The one thing researchers agree on is that Mark Twain did not.

items.why: The line is absent from Twain’s books, letters, and speeches. The curator of the Mark Twain Papers ↗ says “absolutely not,” and no citation to Twain exists before a 2008 tweet.
The anarchist writer is sometimes credited, but like Twain she died long before the slogan surfaced and it appears in none of her published writings or speeches ↗.

items.who: Bob Avakian / Travus T. Hipp / the Berrigans
items.why: The 2003 edition of And I Quote credits RCP chairman Bob Avakian; a Reno newspaper calls it broadcaster Travus T. Hipp’s “typical motto”; and in a 2008 interview Daniel Berrigan credited his brother Philip — none verifiable as the origin ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: an anonymous 20th-century activist slogan — described as “an old anarchist slogan” found as graffiti — that the internet retrofitted onto Mark Twain around 2008 ↗.

context.heading: Why the fake sticks
lead: The line thrives because it flatters cynicism and because Twain’s name lends any epigram instant authority. The irony is that the historical Twain was no voting nihilist: in a 1905 Boston interview he called the ballot “the finest asset we’ve got,” the exact opposite of the sentiment now sold on mugs and shared each election season.

The slogan’s own history is a lesson in how attributions form: an unsigned protest phrase, spray-painted and repeated for decades, gets a famous face bolted on the moment it hits social media — and the face, not the phrase, is what spreads.
context.pull: The real Twain called the ballot box “the finest asset we’ve got.”
